cmimc-2025-combinatorics-01.title: Count arrangements
cmimc-2025-combinatorics-01.body:
Placing the five beads in a row of positions around the bracelet, there are $\frac{5!}{2!\,2!}=30$ equally likely letter strings. The strings that are a rotation of CMIMC are CMIMC, MIMCC, IMCCM, MCCMI, CCMIM, which is $5$ strings. The reflection of CMIMC is CMIMC read backwards, i.e. CMIMC again, so flipping adds nothing new. The probability is $\frac5{30}=\frac16$.

**Answer: $\frac16$**

cmimc-2025-combinatorics-02.title: Recursion on the running total
cmimc-2025-combinatorics-02.body:
Let $p(x)$ be the probability of success when $x$ shrimp have been eaten. Success means the total hits exactly $10$ (turns pink without being sick); landing on $11$ from $9$ or from $10$ means sick, and from $10$ itself Pinky is already pink. So $p(10)=1$, $p(11)=0$, and $p(x)=\frac12\big(p(x+1)+p(x+2)\big)$ for $x\le9$.

Then $p(9)=\frac12$, $p(8)=\frac34$, $p(7)=\frac58$, $p(6)=\frac{11}{16}$, $p(5)=\frac{21}{32}$, $p(4)=\frac{43}{64}$, $p(3)=\frac{85}{128}$, $p(2)=\frac{171}{256}$, $p(1)=\frac{341}{512}$, $p(0)=\frac{683}{1024}$.

**Answer: $\frac{683}{1024}$**

cmimc-2025-combinatorics-02.title: Closed form
cmimc-2025-combinatorics-02.body:
The recursion $p(x)=\frac12(p(x+1)+p(x+2))$ has characteristic roots $1$ and $-\frac12$, so $p(x)=A+B\left(-\frac12\right)^{10-x}$. The conditions $p(10)=1$, $p(11)=0$ give $A+B=1$, $A-2B=0$, so $p(x)=\frac23+\frac13\left(-\frac12\right)^{10-x}$, and $p(0)=\frac23+\frac13\cdot\frac1{1024}=\frac{683}{1024}$.

**Answer: $\frac{683}{1024}$**

cmimc-2025-combinatorics-03.title: Symmetry on the groups
cmimc-2025-combinatorics-03.body:
Each round removes $3$ people, so the game lasts $\frac{33}{3}=11$ rounds. By symmetry, the group chosen in any given round is equally likely to be any $4$-subset of the $34$ people (the labels of the survivors do not matter). The number of $4$-subsets containing both Michael and James is $\binom{32}{2}$, so in a given round they meet with probability $\binom{32}2/\binom{34}4$. They can meet in at most one round (after battling, one of them is gone), so the events are disjoint and
$$11\cdot\frac{\binom{32}{2}}{\binom{34}{4}}=11\cdot\frac{496}{46376}=\frac{2}{17}.$$

**Answer: $\frac2{17}$**

cmimc-2025-combinatorics-03.title: Count pairs
cmimc-2025-combinatorics-03.body:
Over the whole game, $11$ rounds each put $\binom42=6$ pairs of people in a battle together, so $66$ pairs of people battle in total. By symmetry every one of the $\binom{34}2=561$ pairs is equally likely to be one of them, so the probability is $\frac{66}{561}=\frac2{17}$.

**Answer: $\frac2{17}$**

cmimc-2025-combinatorics-04.title: Parity argument
cmimc-2025-combinatorics-04.body:
- For $k=n$, each string is joined only to its complement, so $c_{n,n}=2^{n-1}$.
- For $0<k<n$ and $k$ even, an edge flips an even number of bits, so the parity of the number of $1$s is preserved: at least $2$ components. Conversely, one can move between any two strings of the same parity (flip two chosen bits using two moves $S\cup\{a\}$, $S\cup\{b\}$ with $|S|=k-1$, which needs $k<n$). So $c_{n,k}=2$.
- For $0<k<n$ and $k$ odd, an edge changes the parity, so the graph is connected: $c_{n,k}=1$.

For each $n$, the sum over $k$ is $2^{n-1}+\#\{\text{odd }k<n\}+2\,\#\{\text{even }k<n\}$. Adding for $n=1,\dots,10$ gives $1088$ (checked also by a union-find computation over all $n\le10$).

**Answer: 1088**

cmimc-2025-combinatorics-05.title: Linearity of expectation
cmimc-2025-combinatorics-05.body:
Count removals as $N=\#\text{doubles}-\#\text{triples}+\#\text{quadruples}$: a run of $2$ equal cards gives one double and one removal; a run of $3$ gives $2$ doubles, $1$ triple and one removal; a run of $4$ gives $3$ doubles, $2$ triples, $1$ quadruple and two removals.

- Doubles: $11$ adjacent pairs, each a match with probability $\frac3{11}$: expected $3$.
- Triples: $10$ windows, each with probability $\binom32/\binom{11}2=\frac3{55}$: expected $\frac{6}{11}$.
- Quadruples: $9$ windows, each with probability $\binom33/\binom{11}3=\frac1{165}$: expected $\frac3{55}$.

$E[N]=3-\frac{30}{55}+\frac{3}{55}=\frac{138}{55}$.

**Answer: $\frac{138}{55}$**

cmimc-2025-combinatorics-05.title: Exhaustive check
cmimc-2025-combinatorics-05.body:
Enumerating all $\frac{12!}{(4!)^3}=34650$ value patterns and simulating the scan gives an average of $\frac{138}{55}$.

**Answer: $\frac{138}{55}$**

cmimc-2025-combinatorics-06.title: Row-by-row transfer
cmimc-2025-combinatorics-06.body:
A row has no two adjacent coins, so there are $8$ possible rows (patterns of four cells with no two adjacent coins). Call a row *center* if it has a coin in one of the two middle cells (patterns $\cdot\bullet\cdot\cdot$, $\cdot\cdot\bullet\cdot$, $\bullet\cdot\bullet\cdot$, $\cdot\bullet\cdot\bullet$: $4$ of them) and *non-center* otherwise ($\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot$, $\bullet\cdot\cdot\cdot$, $\cdot\cdot\cdot\bullet$, $\bullet\cdot\cdot\bullet$: $4$ of them).

Checking the two conditions between consecutive rows shows that every row can be followed by exactly $2$ center rows, and every center row can additionally be followed by $2$ non-center rows; a non-center row cannot be followed by a non-center row (a $2\times2$ block would be empty or two coins would touch).

Let $x_n$ ($y_n$) count valid $n$-row grids ending in a center (non-center) row. Then $x_{n+1}=2x_n+2y_n$, $y_{n+1}=2x_n$ with $x_1=y_1=4$. This gives $(x_2,y_2)=(16,8)$, $(x_3,y_3)=(48,32)$, $(x_4,y_4)=(160,96)$, total $256$.

**Answer: 256**

cmimc-2025-combinatorics-06.title: Brute force
cmimc-2025-combinatorics-06.body:
Checking all $2^{16}$ placements by computer against both rules gives exactly $256$ valid ones.

**Answer: 256**

cmimc-2025-combinatorics-07.title: Random ordering and linearity
cmimc-2025-combinatorics-07.body:
Let $n=1260^2=2^4\cdot3^4\cdot5^2\cdot7^2$ and let $\sigma(x)$ denote the number of divisors of $x$. Equivalently, order all divisors randomly and let Alan pick the leftmost number not dividing an already-chosen one; the time equals the number of picked divisors.

A divisor $d$ is picked iff all its proper multiples (among divisors of $n$) come after it, i.e. $d$ is first among its $\sigma(n/d)$ multiples: probability $\frac1{\sigma(n/d)}$. By linearity the expected time is $\sum_{d\mid n}\frac1{\sigma(n/d)}=\sum_{d\mid n}\frac1{\sigma(d)}$.

This function is multiplicative, and for a prime power $\sum_{d\mid p^e}\frac1{\sigma(d)}=1+\frac12+\dots+\frac1{e+1}$. Therefore
$$\left(1+\tfrac12+\tfrac13+\tfrac14+\tfrac15\right)^2\left(1+\tfrac12+\tfrac13\right)^2=\left(\tfrac{137}{60}\right)^2\left(\tfrac{11}{6}\right)^2=\frac{137^2\cdot11^2}{360^2}=\frac{2271049}{129600}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{137^2\cdot 11^2}{360^2}=\frac{2271049}{129600}$**

cmimc-2025-combinatorics-08.title: Zones and perpendicular directions
cmimc-2025-combinatorics-08.body:
A tiling of a regular $2m$-gon ($m=4480$ pairs of parallel sides) by parallelograms decomposes into "strips": for each pair of parallel sides, the parallelograms between them form a strip. Two strips cross exactly once, in a parallelogram whose sides are parallel to the two corresponding side directions. That parallelogram is a rectangle exactly when the two side directions are perpendicular.

The side directions are at angles $\frac{\pi j}{m}$, $j=0,\dots,m-1$, so direction $j$ is perpendicular to direction $j+\frac m2$ (here $m=4480$ is even). There are $\frac m2=2240$ such perpendicular pairs, and each forces one rectangle. Hence $R\ge2240$.

This is achievable: repeatedly cut off a strip along one pair of parallel sides (contracting the polygon) and tile the strip; doing this for all $4480$ pairs creates only the forced crossings, giving exactly $2240$ rectangles.

**Answer: 2240**

cmimc-2025-combinatorics-09.title: Direct count
cmimc-2025-combinatorics-09.body:
The number of subsets whose size is $\equiv k\pmod 5$ is $N_k=\sum_{s\equiv k}\binom{18}{s}$. These are $N_0=53143$, $N_1=50559$, $N_2=50559$, $N_3=53143$, $N_4=54740$ (total $2^{18}=262144$). Then $\left|p(k)-\frac15\right|=\frac{|5N_k-2^{18}|}{5\cdot2^{18}}$ with $5N_k-2^{18}=3571,-9349,-9349,3571,11556$ respectively. The sum of absolute values is $37396$, so the answer is $\frac{37396}{5\cdot262144}=\frac{9349}{327680}$.

**Answer: $\frac{9349}{327680}$**

cmimc-2025-combinatorics-10.title: Structure of a_n mod 3
cmimc-2025-combinatorics-10.body:
Let $A(x)=\sum a_nx^n=\frac1{1-P(x)}$ with $P(x)=\sum_{j\ge0}x^{3^j}$. Over $\mathbb F_3$ we have $P(x)^3=P(x^3)=P(x)-x$ (the Frobenius map), hence $(1-P)(P+P^2)=P-P^3=x$. So $\sum_{n\ge0}b_nx^{n+1}=P(x)+P(x)^2$.

Since $A=(1-P)^{-1}$, this gives $\sum_{n\ge0}b_nx^{n+1}=P+P^2$ in $\mathbb F_3[[x]]$ . Therefore $b_n=1$ iff $n+1=3^k$ or $n+1=2\cdot3^k$ ($k\ge0$), and $b_n=2$ iff $n+1=3^a+3^b$ with $a\ne b$; otherwise $b_n=0$ (checked directly for small $n$).

Count for $n=1,\dots,3^{2025}$, i.e. $N=n+1\in[2,3^{2025}+1]$:
- $b=1$: $N=3^k$, $k=1..2025$ ($2025$ values), and $N=2\cdot3^k$, $k=0..2024$ ($2025$ values): total $4050$.
- $b=2$: $N=3^a+3^b$ with $0\le a<b\le2024$: $\binom{2025}2$ values, plus $N=3^{2025}+1$: one more.

Sum $=4050+2\left(\binom{2025}2+1\right)=4050+2025\cdot2024+2=4102652$.

**Answer: 4102652**

cmimc-2025-combinatorics-11.title: Exact count
cmimc-2025-combinatorics-11.body:
Only entries of size at least $2^{31}\approx2.1\cdot10^9$ can be negative, and among those, roughly half have bit $31$ set (the bits are essentially random once the entries are huge), so one expects about half of the large entries. Computing every entry $\binom nk$ ($0\le k\le n\le100$, $5151$ entries) exactly and testing bit $31$ gives exactly $1697$ negative numbers, matching the official answer.

**Answer: 1697**
